# PQC standards boundary for mdoc signing — 2026-11-25

This note separates published cryptographic **encodings** from the mdoc application and trust rules still selected by CertConcord. It supplements, rather than replaces, [the earlier mdoc source check](standards-research-2026-11-24.md). No full-text assertion is made about the licensed published ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 edition.

## Source status

* [ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 catalog](https://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html): edition 1 was published in September 2021. Its public abstract describes mDL data retrieval, holder binding, origin authentication, and integrity; the complete published text was **not reviewed**. ISO lists a DIS successor under development. No clause below is attributed to the published edition.
* [Public WG10 second-edition CD-ballot-resolution PDF](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ISOWG10/ISO-18013/b250e7a64f99e22ceed10d2a5799bed38ee89f85/Working%20Documents/Working%20Draft%20ISO_IEC_18013-5_second-edition_CD_ballot_resolution_v4.pdf): its cover (PDF p. 1) dates it 2025-09-14 and says the DIS ballot is next. The pinned 2,697,049-byte file was fetched again and SHA-256 checked as `86a1e8356096923bb9293b1582e69193eff724d8fabf7cfe94ef97bf104b3426`. This is **working text**, neither the published 2021 edition nor a verified final DIS. Interior `2021(E)` page headers do not change its status. PDF page references below are one-based PDF pages.
* [NIST FIPS 204](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.204.pdf), §§5.2–5.4: the approved ML-DSA signature primitive, including pure and pre-hash forms. [RFC 9964](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9964.html), §§3, 5, 8.1, is a **published Standards Track RFC** for pure ML-DSA in both COSE and JOSE. [RFC 9881](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9881.html), §§2–5, is a **published Standards Track RFC** for pure ML-DSA in X.509 certificates and CRLs. These standards specify primitives and wire encodings, not a CertConcord issuer or holder authorization policy.

## Exact ML-DSA wire format

| Layer | Published encoding | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| COSE `alg` | `-48` ML-DSA-44, `-49` ML-DSA-65, `-50` ML-DSA-87 | [RFC 9964 §§5, 8.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9964.html#section-8.1.1) |
| Public COSE_Key | `kty: 7` (`AKP`), `alg: -49` or `-50`, `pub: -1` containing the raw ML-DSA public key as a CBOR byte string; no `priv` in a public key | [RFC 9964 §§3, 8.1.2–8.1.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9964.html#section-3) |
| Private COSE_Key | `priv: -2` holds the **32-byte seed**; this is distinct from a 4,032/4,896-byte expanded ML-DSA-65/87 private key | [RFC 9964 §§3–5, 8.1.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9964.html#section-4) |
| JOSE JWK/JWS | JWK `kty: "AKP"`, `alg: "ML-DSA-65"` or `"ML-DSA-87"`, `pub` as base64url of the raw key; private `priv` as base64url of the seed. JWS uses those registered `alg` names and base64url-encodes the signature. | [RFC 9964 §§3, 5, 8.1.4–8.1.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9964.html#section-8.1.4) |
| ML-DSA sizes/mode | ML-DSA-65 public key 1,952 bytes and signature 3,309 bytes; ML-DSA-87 public key 2,592 bytes and signature 4,627 bytes. COSE/JOSE use pure ML-DSA with **empty context**, not HashML-DSA. | [RFC 9964 §§5, 7.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9964.html#section-5); [FIPS 204 §§5.2–5.4](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.204.pdf) |
| X.509 | `id-ml-dsa-44/65/87` algorithm identifiers have absent parameters; ML-DSA public key uses raw encoded key bytes in SPKI `subjectPublicKey` BIT STRING; pure ML-DSA signs DER `TBSCertificate`/CRL with empty context. | [RFC 9881 §§2–4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9881.html#section-2) |

RFC 9881 §5 permits ML-DSA subject keys for signature usages such as `digitalSignature`, `nonRepudiation`, `keyCertSign`, and `cRLSign`, subject to the certificate's actual key usage; it excludes encryption and key agreement usages. RFC 9881 §8.3 excludes HashML-DSA from PKIX certificates/CRLs/OCSP. A certificate's SPKI algorithm and its **issuer signature algorithm** are separate fields; carrying an ML-DSA public key does not itself make the certification path post-quantum. [RFC 9794 §6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9794.html#section-6), an informational terminology RFC, explicitly distinguishes a post-quantum certificate chain from mixed chains and says mixed-chain security needs case-by-case analysis.

## Mdoc and document-signature boundary

| Act | What reviewed standards support | CertConcord PQ implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `issuerAuth` | WG10 §§12.3.1–12.3.5 (PDF pp. 55–59) defines `IssuerAuth = COSE_Sign1` over tagged `MobileSecurityObjectBytes`, issuer certificate in `x5chain`, and protected `alg`. **Its selected issuer algorithms are ES256/ES384/ES512/EdDSA**, not ML-DSA. The reader's issuer certificate, signature, digest, `docType`, and validity checks are in §12.8.1 (PDF p. 70). | RFC 9964 makes an ML-DSA COSE_Sign1 technically defined, but ML-DSA `issuerAuth` is **not selected by this WG10 working text**. A new issuerAuth algorithm or a second PQ signature over the same authenticated MSO needs an explicit experimental extension and verifier rule. An ES256 issuerAuth cannot acquire PQ issuer authenticity merely because it certifies an ML-DSA document key. |
| `DeviceAuth` | WG10 §10.3.3 (PDF p. 37) defines `DeviceSigned` and permits empty `DeviceNameSpaces`. §§12.4.4–12.4.6 (PDF pp. 62–64) signs or MACs tagged `DeviceAuthenticationBytes` containing `SessionTranscript`, `DocType`, and `DeviceNameSpacesBytes`; its device key is the MSO `deviceKeyInfo.deviceKey`. The device signature uses ECDSA/EdDSA curves from Table 17, while the MAC uses ECDH. | `DeviceKey = COSE_Key` in WG10 §12.3.4 is a generic **syntax** reference, but the reviewed §12.4 suite and algorithm rules do **not** authorize an RFC 9964 AKP/ML-DSA key for native `DeviceAuth`. A P-256 DeviceAuth remains classical session proof. Placing a separate AKP document key in an issuer-authenticated application item is experimental and does not turn that key into the mdoc device key. |
| X.509 trust | RFC 9881 standardizes ML-DSA signatures and SPKI; WG10 §12.3.4, §12.8.1, Annex B.1 (PDF pp. 58–59, 70, 84 onward) specify mDL document-signer certificate and validation roles. [RFC 9360 §2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9360.html#section-2) calls carried `x5chain` certificate material untrusted input. | Require an admitted signing trust anchor, correct issuer/certificate role, key usage, document type, validity, and a specified path policy. For a **PQ issuer-authenticity claim**, all authentication edges relied on for that claim must have PQ protection; a traditional certificate-issuer signature or ES256 issuerAuth is a classical dependency. A parallel PQ path or PQ co-signature is a possible new profile, not something RFC 9881 or WG10 automatically supplies. This is a security inference from [RFC 9794 §§5–6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9794.html#section-6). |
| Detached arbitrary-document signature | [RFC 9052 §§4.2–4.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9052.html#section-4.2) standardizes COSE_Sign1 with null payload for separately supplied bytes and `Signature1` over exact protected headers, external AAD, and detached payload. RFC 9964 supplies ML-DSA COSE algorithms. WG10 informative Annex D.7.2 (PDF pp. 151–152) instead illustrates a document hash returned as an authorized `DeviceSigned` element **inside a request/response session**. | A standalone detached ML-DSA COSE document signature uses standardized building blocks, but its document-signing grant, separate certified key, credential binding, critical header contract, and trust decision are **experimental CertConcord profile rules**. Annex D.7.2 is not a detached artifact or a second document key and cannot be cited as one. |

## JOSE/JWT status boundary

ML-DSA JWS **is standardized** by RFC 9964 §§3, 5, 8.1.4; it is incorrect to call all PQ JWT signing an Internet-Draft. That RFC does not specify CertConcord JWT claims, status-list issuer admission, or a PQ upgrade of an ES256-signed JWT. The [Token Status List draft 21](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-status-list/) is still an Internet-Draft in the RFC Editor queue as checked on 2026-11-25; any binding of its JWT status token to this signing profile remains separately selected. An ML-DSA JWS signature on a status token would use a published `alg`, but would not repair a classical `issuerAuth` or classical holder proof.

## Practical decision

The draft-02 P-256 holder/issuer plus ML-DSA document-key design supported only **post-quantum document-signature mathematics under an experimental credential profile**, conditional on classical issuer and holder authentication. Draft 03 separately selects ML-DSA for issuerAuth, its certificate path, holder DeviceSignature, status JWS and the detached document signature, with explicit downgrade rejection. This remains an experimental mdoc algorithm extension, not a claim of ISO mdoc interoperability. Each wire method needs its own authorization and downgrade rules. These are design conclusions from the sources above, not statements about the unreviewed 2021 ISO text.
